Western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) newborns are among the smaller-bodied great ape neonates, with a recorded wet weight at birth of approximately 2061 grams [Wwb = approximately 2061 grams]. This modest initial mass, typical of primates that undergo a prolonged period of maternal investment, sets the stage for a life history characterized by slow growth and delayed maturation. Female gorillas ultimately attain an adult body mass of about 80 kilograms [Wwi = about 80 kilograms], whereas males are considerably more massive, reaching an ultimate wet weight of roughly 157 kilograms [Wwi = roughly 157 kilograms]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism, among the most extreme of any primate species, is closely tied to the species' polygynous mating system and intense male-male competition for access to breeding females. The considerable size advantage enjoyed by silverback males plays a critical role in group defense against predators and rival males, thereby shaping the social structure and reproductive dynamics of wild populations. These life-history parameters, measured across multiple field sites in Central Africa, place the western gorilla at the slow end of the mammalian fast-slow continuum, with implications for population growth rates and the species' vulnerability to environmental perturbations. Gestation in this species lasts for 256 days [tg = 256 days] when measured under the typical body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for the closely related eastern gorilla and reflects the substantial energetic costs of producing a relatively precocial, large-brained neonate.

The pace of reproductive output in western gorilla populations is exceptionally slow, a direct consequence of the species' long interbirth intervals and extended period of offspring dependence. Under optimal conditions at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is equivalent to one surviving infant approximately every 1397 days [Ri = one surviving infant approximately every 1397 days], reflecting the considerable energetic and temporal investment required for each offspring. This low intrinsic rate of increase is characteristic of slow-living primates and renders the species highly sensitive to even modest increases in mortality. The time since birth at weaning for western gorilla infants is 834 days [tx = 834 days], measured at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], marking the end of the period during which the offspring is fully dependent on maternal milk. This extended suckling phase, far longer than in most terrestrial mammals, allows the infant to acquire complex foraging skills and social knowledge from its mother and other group members before achieving nutritional independence. The dense, frugivorous diet of gorillas, which requires extensive knowledge of seasonal fruit availability, likely exerts strong selection pressure favoring this protracted period of maternal provisioning. Weaning weight itself has been documented at 12595 grams [Wwx = 12595 grams], representing a nearly six-fold increase from the average birth mass and reflecting the substantial somatic growth that occurs during this critical developmental window.

Sexual maturation in female western gorillas is a notably late-life event, consistent with the species' overall slow life-history strategy. The time since birth at puberty for females is 2829 days [tp = 2829 days] when measured at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], meaning that females do not typically reach reproductive maturity until approximately 7.75 years of age. This prolonged juvenile period, among the longest documented for any non-human primate, allows ample time for the development of complex social competencies and the accumulation of body mass necessary to support the high energetic demands of gestation and subsequent lactation. Following the attainment of puberty, females typically begin cycling and may conceive their first offspring within one to two years, although the actual age at first successful reproduction is often further delayed by social factors such as female dispersal and the establishment of bonds with a dominant male. The extended interval between birth and sexual maturation means that, even under favorable conditions, population turnover is slow, and a single female may only produce a handful of surviving offspring over her entire lifespan. This demographic pattern has profound implications for the species' ability to recover from population declines caused by habitat loss or disease outbreaks.

Maximum lifespan in wild western gorilla populations has been estimated at 55.4 years [am = 55.4 years] when measured at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], based on long-term observational records from habituated groups in Central Africa. This considerable longevity, comparable to that of chimpanzees and orangutans, underscores the species' position at the extreme slow end of the primate life-history continuum. Such an extended post-reproductive period is relatively rare among mammals and may reflect the adaptive value of older, experienced females who serve as repositories of ecological knowledge regarding seasonal food sources and predator avoidance strategies. In captivity, where veterinary care and consistent nutrition mitigate many of the stochastic mortality risks faced by wild conspecifics, individuals have been documented to survive for over 50 years [am = 50 years], providing additional validation for these field-derived estimates. The combination of late sexual maturation, long gestation, extended interbirth intervals, and a multi-decade lifespan collectively shapes the population dynamics of this species, rendering it particularly vulnerable to any factor that increases adult or juvenile mortality rates above background levels.

The ultimate height length of western gorillas, measured from the crown of the head to the heel in a straightened posture, reaches approximately 155 centimeters [Li = approximately 155 centimeters] in fully grown individuals. This stature, while modest compared to the largest terrestrial mammals, represents a substantial vertical dimension for an arboreally-adapted primate that still spends considerable time on the ground. The species exhibits a relatively short, broad trunk and powerful forelimbs, morphological adaptations that facilitate both terrestrial knuckle-walking and occasional climbing for fruit acquisition. When considered alongside the 256-day gestation period (256 days) [tg = 256 days] measured at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], these morphometric and life-history traits paint a coherent picture of a slow-living, large-bodied primate whose reproductive strategy prioritizes high offspring survival over high fecundity. The combined effect of late puberty, occurring at 2829 days since birth [tp = 2829 days since birth], and the 834-day weaning period (834 days since birth) [tx = 834 days since birth] means that each surviving offspring requires over a decade of maternal investment before reaching full independence at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. Understanding these fundamental biological parameters is critical for constructing accurate population viability models and for designing effective conservation interventions in the face of ongoing threats from poaching, disease, and habitat degradation across the species' remaining range in the lowland forests of Central Africa.
